title: Generative AI in Higher Education: Evidence from an Elite College
extended_summary:
This paper examines how rapidly generative AI has been adopted in higher education and how students are using it academically. The authors focus on key questions about the prevalence of use, which students adopt AI most, whether AI is used mainly to support learning or to automate coursework, how institutional policies shape behavior, and how student beliefs about AI’s benefits relate to adoption. The study responds to widespread debate about generative AI in universities, where policies have often been created without strong empirical evidence.

The study uses a novel student survey administered at Middlebury College, a highly selective liberal arts college in the United States, between December 2024 and February 2025. The analytic sample includes 634 respondents from a student body of about 2,760 undergraduates. The survey collected quantitative data on AI use frequency, purposes of use, beliefs about AI’s effects, and responses to institutional policies, along with open-ended qualitative responses about student experiences and policy views. Because the paper combines survey-based quantitative analysis with qualitative evidence from open-ended responses, it is best characterized as mixed-methods.

The population studied is undergraduate students at a single elite U.S. college. The context is higher education, specifically students’ academic use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude. The authors document very high academic AI adoption: 82.5 percent of students report using generative AI for academic purposes. Adoption differs by discipline, gender, race/ethnicity, and prior academic achievement, with especially high use in natural sciences and among lower-achieving students. Students report using AI more often for augmentation tasks such as explaining concepts, proofreading, and editing than for automation tasks such as essay writing or image creation.

The main conclusions are that generative AI has diffused extremely rapidly in this higher education setting and is already reshaping students’ academic workflows. Students generally perceive AI as improving understanding, learning, and time management, and these beliefs are strongly associated with use. Institutional policies also matter: explicit prohibitions substantially reduce intended use, but students show uneven understanding of AI rules, citation practices, and available institutional resources. The paper argues that blanket policies may have unequal effects across student groups and that more effective governance should distinguish between AI uses that enhance learning and those that risk undermining skill development.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools used by students for academic purposes, including general-purpose chatbots and writing/help systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot, treated in this paper primarily as a broad category rather than a single evaluated product.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed higher-education students about academic adoption, frequency, purposes of use (augmentation vs. automation), beliefs about learning benefits, and responses to institutional AI policies.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of Middlebury College students, 82.5% reported using generative AI for academic purposes during the academic semester, with 23.5% using it rarely, 22.2% occasionally, 26.2% frequently, and 10.6% very frequently. Students reported especially common use for explaining concepts (80.3%), summarizing texts (74.0%), finding information (63.1%), and generating ideas (61.9%).
findings.measure: Self-reported academic AI adoption and task-specific usage frequencies from student survey

findings.finding_summary: Students reported using generative AI more for augmentation than automation: 61.2% of AI users used it for augmentation tasks, versus 41.9% for automation tasks, a 19.3 percentage-point gap. Daily use was also more common for augmentation than automation (5.0% vs. 2.5%), suggesting students more often used AI to support learning processes than to fully automate outputs.
findings.measure: Self-reported augmentation versus automation use across categorized academic tasks

findings.finding_summary: Institutional policy scenarios were associated with large differences in intended AI use. When generative AI use was unrestricted, 52.4% of students said they were likely or extremely likely to use it; under citation-required policies this fell to 40.9%, under no explicit policy to 42.3%, and under explicit prohibition to 13.4%, implying a 37.8 percentage-point decline from unrestricted to banned conditions.
findings.measure: Self-reported likelihood of AI use under alternative institutional policy scenarios
findings.effect_size: 37.8 pp decline under prohibition relative to unrestricted use

findings.finding_summary: Most students believed generative AI improves academic processes: 70.2% said it improves understanding of course materials, 60.1% said it improves learning ability, 59.4% said it improves timely assignment completion, and 41.1% said it improves grades. Beliefs were strongly associated with adoption; a 10-percentage-point increase in belief that AI improves grades corresponded to a 5.6 percentage-point increase in AI adoption, with similar associations for learning ability (4.3 pp), understanding of course materials (4.5 pp), and timely completion (5.3 pp).
findings.measure: Self-reported beliefs about AI impacts on learning, understanding, grades, and time management; association between beliefs and adoption
findings.effect_size: 5.6 pp, 4.3 pp, 4.5 pp, 5.3 pp per 10-pp increase in corresponding belief

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical survey study with descriptive and correlational analyses, not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of learning outcomes. Findings rely primarily on self-reported usage, beliefs, and policy-response intentions from one institution.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper documents large differences in adoption and intended use, but it does not directly estimate causal effects on student learning outcomes with standardized effect sizes. Overall impact on learning is therefore substantial in descriptive terms but unclear in causal educational effect.
